Question: Al, Bert, and Carl are the winners of a school drawing for a pile of Halloween candy, which they are to divide in a ratio of \(3 : 2 : 1,\) respectively. Due to some confusion they come at different times to claim their prizes, and each assumes he is the first to arrive. If each takes what he believes to be his correct share of candy, what fraction of the candy goes unclaimed?
Solution:
Each boy believes the pile he finds is the entire prize, so his share is a fraction of the candy present when he arrives. The ratio has \(3+2+1=6\) equal parts. Al therefore takes \(3/6=1/2\) of his pile, Bert takes \(2/6=1/3\), and Carl takes \(1/6\).

It is easier to track what each boy leaves. Al leaves \(1/2\) of the pile he finds, Bert leaves \(2/3\), and Carl leaves \(5/6\). Each visit multiplies the current amount by its remaining fraction, so the fraction of the original candy left after all three visits is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac56
=\boxed{\frac{5}{18}}.
\]
Changing the arrival order only changes the order of these factors, so the result is the same in every case. The answer is choice D.
